passage: At the community hall on the evening of Nani's eightieth birthday, Sabina had been carrying trays since six. Plates of samosas out, used cups back, wipe the long tables, again. Through the side door she could see Tejas, her younger brother, playing cricket in the car park with the cousins. When she asked Mummy if Tejas could help, an aunty laughed. "Arre, boys don't do all this. He'll only break things." Sabina said nothing. She scraped plates into the bin harder than she needed to, and her feet ached. Then Farhan Mama walked in from the car park, rolled up his sleeves and called, "Tejas! Come, you carry the chairs, I'll wash." Tejas groaned but came. Mama pulled out a chair for Sabina. "Sit. You've done your share and his." Sabina watched her uncle scrub the big pots, and for the first time all evening, she smiled.

qa.q: Since what time had Sabina been carrying trays?
qa.a: Since six.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling while she scraped plates into the bin?
qa.a: She was tired and quietly resentful, noticing that she worked while her brother played and the aunty treated it as normal.

qa.q: How could the family share the work more fairly at the next function?
qa.a: Give every child, boy or girl, a clear job, like Tejas carrying chairs, so the load doesn't fall on Sabina by default.

qa.q: Why might Farhan Mama act differently from the aunty?
qa.a: Farhan Mama seems to believe chores belong to everyone regardless of gender, and he shows it by washing pots himself and calling Tejas in.

grounding: Shows a teenage daughter expected to do more of the work than her brother, noticing the unfairness, and an adult who insists on sharing it.

passage: The school cookery club met on Saturday mornings in the home-science lab, and this week Damini and Shreya were making chicken fried rice. Damini washed her hands with soap before touching anything, then took the red chopping board for the raw chicken and the green one for the vegetables. "Why two boards?" Shreya asked. "Raw chicken juice on the cucumber is how people end up sick," Damini said, and washed the red board and knife in hot soapy water as soon as she was done. She patted the vegetables dry before they went into the oil so it wouldn't spit, and turned the wok handle inwards. When Shreya called from the next counter, "Come look, my rice is stuck!", Damini switched off the gas first, then went. Ms Kapoor, walking past, nodded and moved on to the next table without a word.

qa.q: Which chopping board did Damini use for the raw chicken?
qa.a: The red chopping board.

qa.q: How does Damini seem to feel while she cooks?
qa.a: Damini seems calm and confident, moving through each safe habit without fuss or worry.

qa.q: Which of Damini's habits prevents a burn or fire, and why?
qa.a: Switching off the gas before leaving the stove, drying vegetables before the oil and turning the handle inwards all stop the pan from spitting, catching or being knocked.

qa.q: What might Ms Kapoor's nod and silence suggest about how she sees Damini?
qa.a: Ms Kapoor seems to trust Damini's habits, feeling no need to step in or remind her of anything.

grounding: Illustrates a young cook who washes hands, keeps raw and cooked food apart, handles hot oil carefully and never leaves the lit stove.

passage:
"Kunal, what is that smell?"
"Hi, Rajni didi. Welcome to my room."
"Is that dal? From when?"
"Monday. Maybe Sunday. I was going to wash the pot."
"It's Friday. And why are there clothes on the chair, the bed and the door?"
"Laundry day is Saturday. I was going to do it all then."
"All of it is how much?"
"Basically everything I own." He laughed, then stopped. "Didi, how did it get like this? Two weeks ago it was clean. I didn't do anything."
"That's exactly how. Nothing, every day." She tied her hair up. "Okay. The pot soaks now. You wash your plate the minute you eat. One bucket of clothes every Wednesday, not a mountain on Saturday. And make a list before the shop, or you'll keep buying biscuits and no rice."
"You sound like Ma."
"Ma is right sometimes."

qa.q: Which day did Kunal say the dal was from?
qa.a: Monday, maybe Sunday.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he asked how the room got like this?
qa.a: He was surprised and a bit embarrassed, his laugh stopping as he realised the mess had grown in only two weeks.

qa.q: Which of Rajni's suggestions would stop the pile-up, and why?
qa.a: Washing each plate straight after eating and doing one bucket every Wednesday keeps things small daily, instead of leaving a mountain for Saturday.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel walking into the room?
qa.a: Rajni is probably amused and a little worried, but she treats it kindly and practically, tying her hair up to help rather than scolding.

grounding: Shows a student living away for the first time who is surprised by how fast dishes and laundry pile up, and learns that small daily habits prevent it.

passage: Harsha and Yusuf, both new teachers at the government school in Jhalawar, rented two rooms above a cloth shop. By the third week Harsha had a count in his head. Yusuf's tea glass on the window: washed it. Yusuf's dal pot with the burnt bottom: scrubbed it. Yusuf's plate under the charpai: found it, washed it. Nothing was said. But Harsha began banging the steel pots, sighing loudly, answering Yusuf's jokes with one word. One evening, scraping at the pot again, he nearly said something sharp. Instead he dried his hands, sat down across from Yusuf and said calmly, "Bhai, I've been washing your dishes for three weeks and getting annoyed without telling you. Can we split it? You wash on odd dates, I do even." Yusuf went red. "I thought you didn't mind. You never said." They wrote the rota on the back of a school timetable and stuck it by the tap. The banging stopped.

qa.q: Where did Harsha and Yusuf rent their rooms?
qa.a: Two rooms above a cloth shop in Jhalawar.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling during those three weeks, and how did it show?
qa.a: He was growing resentful, and it came out as banging pots, loud sighs and one-word answers rather than words.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Sitting down and saying calmly what was bothering him, with a simple odd-and-even rota, fixed the problem that weeks of silent anger had not.

qa.q: How did Yusuf see the situation before Harsha spoke?
qa.a: Yusuf honestly thought Harsha didn't mind, so he was embarrassed to learn about the three weeks, going red.

grounding: Shows a flatmate whose resentment grows while silently washing someone else's dishes, until a calm direct word and a rota settle it.

subtype: Routine that keeps a home running [Response]
passage: At the hill school's staff quarters in Mussoorie, Vaibhav knocked on Vinita's door one Wednesday evening to borrow a bucket, and stopped. Her room looked as if nobody had to fight it. The steel plate from dinner was already drying on the rack. A line of clothes swayed over the heater. "Did you just clean for guests?" he asked. Vinita laughed. "No. It's Wednesday, so it's laundry. Sunday after morning duty, I go to the market once, with a list. And I wash the pan while the rice cooks." Vaibhav thought of his own room: a pyramid of shirts, three empty biscuit packets, a mop he had bought and never used. "I clean properly once a month," he said. "All day. Then I hate everything." "I used to do that," she said, handing him the bucket. "Now it's a few minutes a day, and nothing feels like a mountain." That night Vaibhav washed his plate straight after eating.

qa.q: Which day is Vinita's laundry day?
qa.a: Wednesday.

qa.q: How does Vinita seem to feel about keeping her room?
qa.a: Vinita seems relaxed and at ease, laughing at the question, because her small routines keep the room from ever becoming a mountain.

qa.q: What small step could Vaibhav keep up after that evening?
qa.a: Keep washing his plate right after eating, then add one fixed laundry day, instead of saving everything for a monthly all-day clean.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel standing in Vinita's doorway?
qa.a: Vaibhav is surprised, a little envious and perhaps embarrassed, comparing her calm room with his own pile of shirts and biscuit packets.

grounding: Illustrates an adult whose few fixed habits, cleaning as she cooks, one weekly shop and a set laundry day, keep her home running with little stress.

passage: At the Dussehra mela in Delhi, Mahima could see only backs and elbows, and held Aditi Masi's hand so hard her knuckles went white. At the gate, Masi had crouched and said, "Say Papa's number." Mahima said all ten digits. "And if we lose each other?" "I go to the big ice-cream stall by the gate and tell the ice-cream uncle or a police aunty." Near the giant Ravan, crackers burst, people surged, and Masi's hand slipped away. Mahima's chest went tight; she wanted to cry and run. Instead she found the stall's blue umbrella and told the man there, "I'm lost. My papa's number is..." He dialled while she stood beside his cart. Ten minutes later Masi pushed through, breathless, and hugged her so hard her hair clip fell off.

qa.q: Where had Mahima agreed to go if they got separated?
qa.a: To the big ice-cream stall by the gate.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when Masi's hand slipped away?
qa.a: She was frightened; her chest went tight and she wanted to cry and run.

qa.q: What made Mahima safe once she was lost?
qa.a: Practising Papa's number and a meeting place at the gate gave her something to do instead of panicking, so she went straight to the stall and asked for help.

qa.q: What was it like for Aditi Masi during those ten minutes?
qa.a: Aditi Masi was probably terrified while searching, and then deeply relieved, hugging Mahima so hard that the hair clip fell off.

grounding: Shows a child anxious about getting lost in a crowd, kept safe by knowing a parent's number and a pre-agreed place to wait.

passage: Esther had checked her ticket five times before the Galway bus even left Dublin. Seat 14, window. Mum had written the plan on a card in her jacket pocket: text at Athlone, text at Ballinasloe, Uncle Javier waiting at Galway bus station, call him if anything changes. She was fourteen and had never gone this far alone. For the first hour she mostly watched the green fields slide past, grinning at nothing. Then the driver announced a twenty-minute delay for roadworks, and her stomach dropped. Would Javier leave? She read the card again, then texted: "Delay 20 min, still on bus, all ok." He replied at once: "No rush. I'll get a coffee 🙂" At Ballinasloe she checked the ticket again, just in case. When the bus finally pulled in, Javier stood by the door holding a sign that said ESTHER in huge letters, and she pretended to be embarrassed.

qa.q: Where did Mum's card say Esther should send texts?
qa.a: At Athlone and at Ballinasloe.

qa.q: How did Esther feel when the delay was announced?
qa.a: Her excitement turned to worry; her stomach dropped and she feared Javier might leave.

qa.q: What made the trip manageable for a first solo journey?
qa.a: The route and a contact person were agreed on the card, so when the delay came Esther knew exactly what to do: text Javier.

qa.q: How might Uncle Javier feel waiting at the bus station?
qa.a: Javier seems relaxed and proud, calm about the delay and playful with the big sign to welcome her.

grounding: Shows a teenager on a first solo journey, excited and a little afraid, kept steady by an agreed route and a contact person.

passage: "Sharmila, you're off on your first work trip, so let your Swati aunty tell you about mine. I was twenty-five, going to a training in Guwahati. My father made me do dull things the night before: two photocopies of my ID, one in the suitcase, one in my shoe bag; the ticket printed and also emailed to myself; my manager's number and the hotel's number on paper, not only in the phone. And he said, reach two hours early and know which train to take if the flight goes. Well. Fog. Flight cancelled. People were shouting at the counter. I went straight to the station, because I had the night train written down. Then at the station someone lifted my wallet. Real ID gone. The copy in my shoe bag got me on that train, and the paper numbers let me call the hotel. I arrived tired, not stranded. That's all preparation does, beta. It makes the bad day smaller."

qa.q: Where was young Swati's second ID photocopy?
qa.a: In her shoe bag.

qa.q: How might young Swati have felt when her wallet was stolen at the station?
qa.a: She was probably shocked and scared for a moment, then relieved to remember the copy in her shoe bag.

qa.q: Which of young Swati's preparations turned out to matter most, and why?
qa.a: The spare ID copy and the numbers on paper, because once the wallet was gone they were what got her on the train and in touch with the hotel.

qa.q: How might the people shouting at the counter have experienced the cancellation differently?
qa.a: Without a backup plan, they were stuck and angry, while Swati already knew her next step and went straight to the station.

grounding: Illustrates a traveller who keeps documents and contacts in two places, arrives early and has a backup route, so a cancellation and a theft become only an inconvenience.
